subtitle: Ageism affects both younger and older people. You will learn to recognize it, apply federal and Minnesota age protections at the right level, and replace generational stereotypes with individual, person-centered practice.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including those who work with coworkers, partners and people served across the age span. It builds shared language and does not replace HR, EOAD or legal advice.

lessons.title: What ageism is and why it matters
objectives: Explain the World Health Organization's three-part description of ageism: stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination.
Distinguish institutional, interpersonal and self-directed ageism with a workplace example of each.
Identify ways ageism affects both younger and older people.
Describe the limits of global survey evidence on ageism.
lessons.teaching:
Age assumptions can shape how people understand another person’s interests, skills and experience. The World Health Organization describes three parts of ageism: stereotypes in how people think, prejudice in how they feel and discrimination in how they act. These can be directed toward other people or toward oneself. The concern is how age-based judgments contribute to harm, disadvantage or unfair treatment.

Ageism can appear in rules, interactions and beliefs about oneself. A workplace might steer learning opportunities toward younger staff without checking the interests of others. A colleague might dismiss someone’s ideas because they seem too young, or joke that an older coworker cannot learn. People may also absorb such messages and decide they are too old to apply or too young to be taken seriously. These examples illustrate possible barriers; an individual decision still needs to be examined in context.

Younger people can face age-based barriers as well as older adults. WHO describes limits on younger workers’ opportunities to contribute to decisions, alongside patronizing treatment across age groups. A team can examine whether it assumes that a newer employee cannot lead or that someone nearing retirement has no interest in development. Relevant experience may matter for an assignment, but age alone does not establish skill, interest or readiness.

WHO’s 2021 report release described survey responses from 83,034 people in 57 countries. About half held moderately or highly ageist attitudes toward older people, according to the measure used. This finding describes surveyed attitudes; it does not establish the rate of biased decisions at DHS or diagnose any colleague. WHO also describes associations between ageism, poorer health and social isolation, which should not be treated as proof about a particular person’s health. For team practice, examine the actual decision and ask what evidence supports it. Invite people to state their interests instead of assuming them from age, appearance or years of service.
lessons.keyPoint: Ageism is stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination based on age, aimed at others or at oneself. It affects younger and older people and shows up in rules, interactions and self-talk.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD unit is choosing someone to learn a new contract management system and train others. The supervisor, Aurelio, says in a meeting that Dagny, who has twenty-five years in the unit, probably would not want to deal with new software, and suggests Kip, the newest hire, because younger people pick up technology faster. Dagny has not been asked. Kip is also not sure he wants the role.
lessons.question: What would be a better approach for Aurelio?
choices: Assign both Dagny and Kip so no one feels left out.
Keep his choice, since it is only a training assignment and not a promotion.
Describe what the role involves, invite interest from everyone on the team, and choose based on interest and job-related factors rather than assumptions about age.
feedback: Assigning both may seem fair, but it still skips asking people what they want and still rests on assumptions about them.
Training and assignments are exactly where small age assumptions add up. The EEOC lists job assignments and training among the employment decisions covered by age discrimination law.
This is the best response. It removes age assumptions about both Dagny and Kip and makes the decision about interest and the work.
lessons.reflection: Think about a time you assumed something about a coworker based on their age, older or younger. What did you assume, and how did you find out whether it was true?
lessons.action: When assigning work, distinguish actual experience from assumptions about age. If a comment links age to ability or interest, identify the job-related evidence needed to assess the person fairly.

check.question: According to the World Health Organization, which set best describes the parts of ageism?
check.correct: Stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination based on age, directed toward others or oneself.
wrong: Only discrimination against people over sixty-five.
Only illegal employment decisions based on age.
check.feedback: WHO's description covers thoughts, feelings and actions, and it includes ageism toward younger people and ageism people direct at themselves. Legal protections are one part of the picture, not the whole of it.

lessons.title: Age protections at work: federal and Minnesota law
objectives: Describe who is protected under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act.
Explain how Minnesota Human Rights Act age protection differs from the federal law.
Identify common workplace comments and practices that can signal age bias.
Identify where to raise a concern about age discrimination or harassment.
lessons.teaching:
Two laws matter most for age at work in a Minnesota state agency. The federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act protects people age forty and older. The usual twenty-employee threshold applies to private employers; state and local government employers are covered regardless of size. Covered decisions include hiring, pay, assignments, promotion, training and benefits. Harassment based on age is also unlawful when it is so frequent or severe that it creates a hostile work environment or leads to an adverse decision. The EEOC explains that the ADEA does not prohibit favoring an older worker over a younger one, even when both are forty or older. That federal distinction does not authorize a Minnesota agency to ignore broader state protections.

The Minnesota Human Rights Act goes further. Minnesota Statutes section 363A.03 says the prohibition against age discrimination in employment protects a person over the age of majority, with a separate rule for educational practices under section 363A.13 covering people over twenty-five. In practice, that means state law protects younger adult workers from age discrimination in employment too, not only people over forty. Statewide human resources policy follows this broader coverage.

Age assumptions may appear in language that sounds complimentary or practical. Phrases such as we need fresh energy, a digital native, overqualified, not a long-term investment, or will not be around long enough to make this worthwhile can signal that age is influencing a decision. So can practices like offering conferences and training mostly to newer staff, assuming someone near retirement is not interested in a stretch assignment, or treating a younger colleague's ideas as inexperience. Jokes about age, repeated nicknames about age and comments about someone's energy or memory can contribute to a hostile environment.

None of this means every decision involving people of different ages is suspect. The question is whether the decision rests on job-related facts or on assumptions about age. If you notice a pattern, or someone brings you a concern, you do not need to determine whether it is illegal. Employees can raise age concerns with a supervisor, HR or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division, and externally with the Minnesota Department of Human Rights or the EEOC. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the agency affirmative action officer. Follow DHS referral and protection procedures without waiting for a repeated incident or making an independent legal determination.
lessons.keyPoint: Federal law protects workers forty and older. Minnesota law protects adult workers of any age from age discrimination in employment. Watch for decisions that rest on age assumptions rather than job-related facts.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD hiring panel is reviewing finalists for a policy specialist role. One panelist, Gideon, says a strong candidate, Rosamund, is probably overqualified and will retire soon, so the unit should pick someone who will stay. Another panelist, Nerys, says a different candidate seems too young to handle county partners. The panel chair, Idris, notices that both comments are about age, not about the job criteria. Idris has already made the required immediate report and is following HR’s direction while correcting the panel discussion.
lessons.question: What should Idris do?
choices: Redirect the panel to the posted job criteria and evidence from the interviews, note that assumptions about retirement or youth should not factor in, and consult HR if the concern continues.
Let each panelist score as they see fit, since panel members are entitled to their views.
Remove both candidates from consideration to avoid any appearance of bias.
feedback: Idris has already reported the concern. He should keep the panel focused on documented job criteria and follow HR’s direction; the option’s reference to further consultation is not permission to postpone the initial report.
Panelists use judgment, but comments tying a candidate's suitability to age can signal age discrimination under federal and state law. The chair has a responsibility to redirect them.
Removing qualified candidates would be its own unfair decision. The problem is the reasoning, not the candidates.
lessons.reflection: Which age-related phrases have you heard in hiring, assignments or feedback that seemed harmless at the time? How might they sound to the person being described?
lessons.action: Review one assignment or training decision against its job-related criteria. Identify possible age assumptions and follow the applicable reporting process for concerns; do not investigate allegations through a learning exercise.

check.question: How does Minnesota Human Rights Act age protection in employment differ from the federal ADEA?
check.correct: Minnesota law protects adults over the age of majority, not only those forty and older.
wrong: Minnesota law protects only people over sixty-five.
Minnesota law does not cover age at all.
check.feedback: The ADEA begins at forty. Minnesota Statutes section 363A.03 extends employment age protection to adults over the age of majority, so younger adult workers are also protected under state law.

lessons.title: Multigenerational teams without generational stereotypes
objectives: Summarize what the National Academies found about the evidence for generational differences at work.
Distinguish age effects, period effects and generational effects.
Explain why generational labels can become a proxy for age.
Plan team practices that respond to individual needs instead of generational categories.
lessons.teaching:
Advice about workplace generations often assigns a shared personality to people born during a particular period. One group is described as loyal, another as needing praise, and another as independent. Such labels may sound familiar, but they cannot reliably tell a manager what a particular employee needs or values.

A 2020 National Academies committee reviewed the evidence and advised against using generational categories to manage workers. Much of the research cannot separate age effects, period effects and cohort effects. Age effects concern changes as people grow older; period effects concern wider changes affecting people across ages. Cohort effects concern shared influences on a particular group. Comparing younger and older staff at one point in time cannot, by itself, separate those explanations. The committee found substantial variation within age groups and warned that labels can encourage stereotypes or serve as a substitute for age in employment decisions.

For a DHS team, the practical response is to ask about individual needs while maintaining clear work expectations. Discuss how each person prefers to receive feedback and what support would help with a new system. Offer usable learning options without assuming that age determines technical skill or confidence. A shared baseline can provide consistent expectations while allowing adjustments for different tasks and circumstances. Staff need not disclose personal health or family details to discuss ordinary work support; accommodation requests follow the appropriate process.

WHO identifies contact between age groups as one strategy for reducing ageism, alongside education and policy or legal measures. Reciprocal mentoring and shared projects are possible applications when they have clear purposes, approved time and accessible participation. Do not assume that one activity will change attitudes, or that someone should teach others because of their age. Assign leadership according to the work and appropriate authority, and ask participants whether the arrangement is useful. The aim is to learn about colleagues through their contributions and stated needs rather than a generational label.
lessons.keyPoint: Strong evidence for generational differences in work values is lacking. Respond to individual needs and life circumstances, not generational labels, and build contact across ages through shared work.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD communications unit is redesigning how it gives feedback on drafts. The manager, Octavia, shares an article claiming that younger staff need frequent praise while older staff prefer to be left alone, and proposes two separate feedback schedules by age group. Cyrus, a senior writer, and Tove, a recent hire, both find the idea awkward. Octavia sincerely wants to meet everyone's needs.
lessons.question: What would be the most effective approach for Octavia?
choices: Use the two schedules, since the article is based on research.
Ask each team member how and how often they want feedback, set a shared baseline for everyone and adjust individually.
Drop the redesign and keep the current approach to avoid controversy.
feedback: The National Academies found little strong evidence for generational differences in work values, and dividing feedback by age risks treating people differently because of age.
This is the best response. It meets real individual needs, applies a common standard and avoids sorting people by age.
Avoiding the change leaves any real feedback problems unsolved. The issue is the method, not the goal.
lessons.reflection: What generational label have you applied to yourself or others? What does it explain, and what might it hide about the individual?
lessons.action: Next time you plan a change that affects your team, such as a new tool or process, ask each person what support they would find useful rather than predicting by age or experience.

check.question: Why did the National Academies committee caution against using generational categories to manage workers?
check.correct: Evidence for generational differences in work values is weak, and categorizing workers can lead to overgeneralization and discrimination.
wrong: Because generational differences are so large that they cannot be managed.
Because federal law prohibits discussing generations at work.
check.feedback: The committee found that apparent generational differences often reflect age or period effects. It recommended focusing on individual needs and the context of work. Generational labels can also stand in for age, which raises discrimination risks.

lessons.title: Age in service delivery
objectives: Describe the federal Age Discrimination Act and the kinds of programs it covers.
Distinguish lawful age-based eligibility set in statute from age-based assumptions in service.
Identify examples of ageist practice when working with older adults and young people.
Plan a person-centered alternative to an age-based assumption in a service interaction.
lessons.teaching:
Age shapes service delivery as well as the workplace. A federal law, the Age Discrimination Act, prohibits discrimination on the basis of age in programs and activities that receive federal financial assistance. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services explains that it protects people of all ages, not only older adults. Many DHS programs and the county and provider programs DHS funds receive federal funds. Employment practices are generally excluded from this Act; employment protections were addressed in the earlier lesson.

The Act also recognizes that some programs lawfully use age. Age distinctions set by federal, state or local statute, such as an eligibility age written into law, continue to apply, and HHS describes other narrow exceptions for factors that are necessary to a program's normal operation or that are reasonable factors other than age. So the question is not whether age ever appears in a program. It is whether staff are adding age-based assumptions that the program's rules do not require. Formal questions about whether a program's age distinctions are lawful go to DHS legal counsel and the civil rights office.

Assumptions show up in small moments. Staff may speak to an older person's adult child instead of the person, assume an older adult cannot use an online portal, use a slow, sing-song tone sometimes called elderspeak, or describe an older person's preferences as confusion. With young adults, including young people with disabilities moving from children's to adult services, staff may assume they are too young to make choices about where to live or work, or talk mostly to parents. In disability services, age assumptions can mix with disability assumptions, which makes them harder to see.

The alternative is person-centered practice, which DSD programs already expect. Speak first to the person the service is for. Ask how they prefer to receive information and offer more than one channel rather than assuming by age. Ask who, if anyone, they want involved in decisions. Respect the person’s preferences and check any applicable legal representative’s authority, consent requirements and safety duties. Age or disability alone does not establish that someone else can decide for the person. When an age-based rule does apply, explain it plainly as a program rule, not a judgment about the person. These habits also help in workplace interactions with coworkers of every age.
lessons.keyPoint: Lawful program age rules apply as written, but staff should not add age assumptions of their own. Speak to the person, ask their preferences and offer choices, for older adults and young people alike.
lessons.example: Practice case: Philippa, a county case manager working with DSD guidance, meets with Bertrand, who is seventy-eight and has a disability, about changing his services. His daughter, Linnea, attends. Philippa directs most questions to Linnea and suggests paper forms because online tools can be confusing at his age. Bertrand, who manages his own email and online banking, grows quiet. Later a DSD staff member reviewing the case notes the pattern. Bertrand makes his own service decisions, and Linnea is attending as a support person at his request.
lessons.question: What should Philippa do differently in the next meeting?
choices: Continue addressing Linnea, since family members often know best.
Ask Bertrand to demonstrate that he can use the online tools before offering them.
Speak directly to Bertrand, ask how he prefers to receive information and how he wants Linnea involved, and offer both online and paper options.
feedback: In this case, Linnea is a support person and Bertrand makes his own decisions. In other cases, verify the scope of any legal representative’s authority while continuing to involve the person receiving services.
Asking him to prove his ability singles him out because of age. Offering options and asking preferences works for everyone.
This is the best response. It is person-centered, respects Bertrand's choices about family involvement and removes an age-based assumption about technology.
lessons.reflection: In your work with the public or with partners, when might you default to assumptions about what someone can do or wants based on how old they seem? What question could replace the assumption?
lessons.action: Review one standard letter, form or intake script you use. Check whether it assumes a preferred channel or decision-maker by age, and suggest a change that offers the person a choice.

check.question: Whom does the federal Age Discrimination Act protect in federally funded programs?
wrong: Only people age forty and older.
Only people age sixty-five and older.
check.feedback: HHS explains that the Act applies to persons of all ages in programs receiving federal financial assistance. The age forty threshold belongs to the ADEA, which covers employment.

cards.back: Stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination toward others or oneself based on age, as described by the World Health Organization.
The federal employment law protecting people age forty and older. Private-employer coverage generally starts at twenty employees; state and local government employers are covered regardless of size.
Minnesota Human Rights Act employment protection against age discrimination for adults over the age of majority.
A change that affects people of all ages at the same time, such as new technology. It is often mistaken for a generational difference.
A federal law prohibiting age discrimination against people of any age in programs receiving federal financial assistance, with exceptions for age rules set in statute.

aid.heading: Checking a workplace decision for age assumptions
items: List the job-related criteria before discussing people.
Watch for phrases like fresh energy, digital native, overqualified or close to retirement.
Offer training and stretch work across career stages.
Ask people about their interests instead of predicting by age.
Follow reporting requirements promptly; supervisors and managers must immediately report protected-class allegations through the required channels.

aid.heading: Working across ages on a team
items: Ask each person how they like to receive feedback and information.
Offer more than one way to learn new tools.
Use two-way mentoring and mixed-experience project teams.
Replace generational labels with questions about individual needs.

aid.heading: Age in service interactions
items: Speak first to the person the service is for.
Ask who the person wants involved and verify any legal representative’s actual authority.
Offer online and paper or phone options without assuming.
Explain age-based program rules as rules, not judgments.
Route questions about the lawfulness of age rules to legal counsel or the civil rights office.

sources.title: World Health Organization — Ageing: Ageism (questions and answers)
sources.note: Supports the description of ageism as stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination toward others or oneself, the institutional, interpersonal and self-directed forms, and effects on younger people.

sources.title: World Health Organization — Ageism is a global challenge: UN (news release on the Global Report on Ageism, 2021)
sources.note: Supports the definition from the global report, the one-in-two survey finding and the three strategies of policy and law, education and intergenerational contact. Survey findings describe attitudes, not individual workplaces.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Age Discrimination
sources.note: ADEA age coverage, employment decisions and harassment; use the accompanying Supreme Court decision for state and local government employer coverage.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 363A.03 — Definitions (Minnesota Human Rights Act)
sources.note: Supports that Minnesota employment age protection covers people over the age of majority. Formal determinations rest with MDHR and the courts.

sources.title: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine — Are Generational Categories Meaningful Distinctions for Workforce Management? (Summary, 2020)
sources.note: Supports the finding that evidence for generational differences in work values is weak, the age, period and cohort distinction, and the recommendation to focus on individual needs.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Age in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance
sources.note: Supports that the Age Discrimination Act protects people of all ages in federally assisted programs, excludes most employment practices and allows age distinctions set by statute and other narrow exceptions.

sources.title: U.S. Supreme Court — Mount Lemmon Fire District v. Guido (2018)
sources.note: State and local government employers are covered by the ADEA regardless of workforce size.

sources.title: 45 CFR Part 91 — HHS age discrimination regulations
sources.note: Current scope and exceptions for age distinctions in federally assisted programs; formal interpretation belongs to the responsible legal and civil-rights functions.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations to Human Resources or the agency affirmative action officer.

sources.note: Describes employee reporting, supervisory protection and prompt referral responsibilities, and designated Equal Opportunity and Access functions.
